claims.text: The nanoparticles are smaller than 10 nm.
The nanoparticles contain equiatomic Au, Co, Cu, Ni, and Pt.
The initial nanoparticles are a single-phase solid solution.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down above 600 K in these nanoparticles.
Above the breakdown temperature, surface-energy minimization dominates configurational-entropy stabilization.
Au and Cu are the low-surface-energy constituents of this quinary alloy.
Heating drives rapid segregation of Au and Cu to nanoparticle surfaces.
Ostwald ripening causes the loss of the smallest nanoparticles.
The high surface-to-volume ratio makes surface-energy terms dominant in sub-10 nm particles.
Surface diffusion coefficients in these nanoparticles are enhanced relative to bulk diffusion coefficients.
Small particle size reduces the activation energy for surface diffusion.
A sufficiently strong thermodynamic driving force can produce segregation or phase separation despite sluggish-diffusion-based stabilization in high-entropy alloys.
Surface and interfacial energy reduction overcomes the kinetic barrier from sluggish bulk diffusion in Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles.
The resulting mass transport is rapid relative to transport in bulk versions of the alloy.
Heating produces substantial shape evolution toward faceted or spherical morphologies governed by surface-energy anisotropy.
Heating produces an Au/Cu-enriched surface skin and a Co/Ni/Pt-enriched core.
High configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion are proposed in high-entropy-alloy theory to suppress segregation or precipitate growth.
Those baseline effects would maintain the equiatomic single phase and particle-size distribution up to 1000 K.
Surface-controlled evolution applies below 10 nm, whereas above 50 nm bulk sluggish diffusion remains rate limiting.
The cited refractory-alloy coating evidence demonstrates surface segregation in another alloy system.
